titleStmt.title: What are the differences between long-term, short-term, and working memory?
titleStmt.author: Cowan

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: What are the differences between long-term, short-term, and working memory?

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the three terms long-term, short-term and working memory, and whether the distinctions drawn between them are substantive or terminological
span.quote: In the recent literature there has been considerable confusion about the three types of memory: long-term, short-term, and working memory.

span.label: do short-term and long-term memory differ in kind — in temporal decay and chunk capacity — and is the further distinction between short-term and working memory a real one
span.quote: Long- and short-term memory could differ in two fundamental ways, with only short-term memory demonstrating (1) temporal decay and (2) chunk capacity limits.

span.label: separates the substantive question (is there decay, is there a capacity limit) from the terminological one (what shall we call the attention-related part), and concludes the second is a matter of usage while the first is not
span.quote: In sum, the question of whether short-term memory and working memory are different may be a matter of semantics.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Thus, we can say that short-term memory exists, but often without great clarity as to whether the limit is a time limit or a chunk capacity limit.

span.label: short-term, long-term and working memory distinctions
span.quote: In the recent literature there has been considerable confusion about the three types of memory: long-term, short-term, and working memory.

span.label: review
span.quote: In this chapter I will assess the strength of evidence for three types of memory: long-term memory, short-term memory, and working memory.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Short-term memory arises as a temporarily activated subset of long-term memory, part of which falls within a capacity-limited focus of attention
span.quote: In this framework, short-term memory is derived from a temporarily activated subset of information in long-term memory.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Attention freed by an undemanding distractor task is used for an attention-based rehearsal that refreshes items, so recall falls as the distractor rate consumes that attention
span.quote: The notion is that when the distracting task does not require attention, the freed-up attention allows an attention- based rehearsal of the items to be recalled.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Working memory tasks correlate with aptitude because preventing covert rehearsal forces reliance on attention-demanding storage and processing
span.quote: According to this view, what may be necessary for a working memory procedure to correlate well with cognitive aptitudes is that the task must prevent covert verbal rehearsal so that the participant must rely on more attention-demanding processing and/or storage to carry out the task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A post-perceptual mask overwrites sensory-specific features in activated memory, leaving only categorical information inside the attention-protected focus
span.quote: Presumably, the mask was capable of overwriting various types of sensory-specific features in activated memory, leaving behind only the more generic, categorical information present in the focus of attention, which presumably is protected from masking interference by the attention process.

span.label: the whole argument is organised as contamination control: for each claimed property of short-term memory, name the confounds that could produce the same result, then ask which studies defeated them
span.quote: To assess decay one must take into account, or overcome, contaminating effects of rehearsal, long-term retrieval, and temporal distinctiveness, which will be discussed one at a time in conjunction with evidence for and against decay.

span.label: a nuisance parameter is varied by four-fold across two modalities and the limit does not move, which converts an ambiguous number into a capacity rather than a rate
span.quote: Given the striking differences between Sperling and Darwin et al. in the time period available for the transfer of information to a categorical form, the common four-item limit is best viewed as a capacity limit rather than a rate limit.

span.label: a cross-modal additivity prediction is used as the test: if one store holds everything, two modalities together cannot exceed the larger single modality alone
span.quote: Moreover, if the cross-modality, capacity-limited store were the only type of storage used, then the sum of visual and auditory capacities in the dual-modality condition should be no greater than the larger of the two unimodal capacities (which happened to be the visual capacity).

span.label: the confound is designed out of the experiment rather than corrected for: one trial per participant, gathered by putting the laboratory in a shopping mall
span.quote: Baddeley and Scott (1971) set up a trailer in a shopping mall so that they could test a large number of participants for one trial each, so as to avoid proactive interference.

span.label: chunking is neutralised by choosing tasks in which grouping is impossible — an unpredictable list end, or a four-per-second rate — rather than by trying to measure the chunks
span.quote: For example, in running memory span, a long list of items is presented with an unpredictable endpoint, making grouping impossible.

span.label: the chunk is made observable by defining it operationally through the participant's own output rather than by the experimenter's guess about grouping
span.quote: A chunk was defined as a series of words reproduced by the participant in the same order in which the words had been presented.

span.label: a masking step is used to strip away everything except the contested store, so that what remains is the thing being measured
span.quote: Presumably, the mask was capable of overwriting various types of sensory-specific features in activated memory, leaving behind only the more generic, categorical information present in the focus of attention, which presumably is protected from masking interference by the attention process.

span.label: a post-stimulus retention cue splits encoding from maintenance, so the modality-specific and modality-general phases can be measured in the same trial
span.quote: The part of working memory preceding the cue showed modality-specific dual-task effects: encoding a stimulus set of one type was hurt more by also encoding another set if both sets were in the same modality.

span.label: a warning against reading a box diagram as an ontology: the boxes record the order in which information arrives, not places where memory exclusively lives
span.quote: these boxes do not imply that memory is exclusively in one box or another; they are better interpreted as the relative times of the first entry of information from a stimulus into one store and then the next

span.label: the paper demonstrates its own subject matter on the reader inside a parenthesis, using sentence structure to load the reader's working memory
span.quote: (Your working memory would have been more heavily taxed while reading the previous sentence if I had saved the phrase “one relies on working memory” until the end of the sentence, which I did in within my first draft of that sentence; working memory thus affects good writing.)

span.label: a mathematical model separates two stores by assuming their contributions are independent, S+L−SL; the paper then reports that the data fit a complementary-resource assumption better
span.quote: This model assumes that, for any particular serial position within a list, the likelihood of successful short-term storage (S) and long-term storage (L) are independent, so that the likelihood of recalling the item is S+L−SL.

span.label: a patient dissociation is used to identify which store a response came from: Korsakoff amnesia spares the last few serial positions in immediate recall and not in delayed recall
span.quote: These studies show that, in immediate recall, performance in amnesic individuals is preserved at the last few serial positions of the list.

span.label: decay is reconceived from a gradual fade to a sudden collapse at a trial-varying point, which changes what an averaged curve is evidence for
span.quote: It may be that decay actually reflects not a gradual degradation of the quality of the short-term memory trace, but a sudden collapse at a point that varies from trial to trial.

span.label: rehearsal is split into two kinds so that the standard control is shown to be incomplete: articulatory suppression stops the covert-speech kind and leaves the attention-based kind untouched
span.quote: The key difference is that it would not be expected that articulatory suppression would prevent that type of rehearsal. Instead, to prevent that type of rehearsal an attention-demanding task would have to be used.

span.label: Both of the properties on which the short-term/long-term distinction rests remain controversial
span.quote: Both properties of short-term memory are still controversial but the current literature is rather encouraging regarding the existence of both decay and capacity limits.

span.label: Decay in particular is left unresolved by the review
span.quote: The question of decay is still pretty much open to debate, whereas there is growing support for a chunk capacity limit.

span.label: How time limits and chunk capacity limits jointly govern recall is not settled
span.quote: The exact way in which these limits work together is not yet clear.

span.label: the decay claim is still not secure after fifty years of work
span.quote: Still, it seems that the concept of decay is not yet on very firm ground and warrants further study.

span.label: the two limits cannot be cleanly separated even when both are granted
span.quote: Thus, we can say that short-term memory exists, but often without great clarity as to whether the limit is a time limit or a chunk capacity limit.

span.label: the number of chunks used in recall is not usually observable, so the capacity number is not directly measurable
span.quote: Because it is not usually clear what chunks have been used in recall, it is not clear how many chunks can be retained and whether the number is truly fixed.

span.label: a design in which the grouping variable is also the grouping measure — Vogel et al. split participants by the very signal being compared
span.quote: One limitation of the study is that the separation of participants into high versus low span was based on the CDA also, and the task used to measure the CDA inevitably required selective attention (to one half of the display) on every trial, whether or not it included objects of an irrelevant color.

span.label: the interpretation of the working-memory/aptitude correlation, the field's main reason for using the term, is unsettled
span.quote: However, more research is needed on exactly what we learn from the high correlation between working memory and intellectual aptitudes

span.label: a proposed decay experiment is conceded in advance to be reinterpretable as interference, so the design cannot settle the question
span.quote: Unfortunately, though, such results might be accounted for alternatively as the result of interference from the distracting stimuli, without the need to invoke decay.

span.label: how the capacity limit and the time limit combine is left unresolved
span.quote: The exact way in which these limits work together is not yet clear.

span.label: the practical demand that created the modern short-term memory task — operators holding rapid dot-dash series, then subscriber numbers — which the paper offers as the ecological source of the nonsense-syllable laboratory
span.quote: The nonsense syllables that Ebbinghaus had invented as a tool can be seen to have acquired more ecological validity in an industrial age with expanding information demands, perhaps highlighting the practical importance of primary memory in daily life.

span.label: the cell assembly, imported to give short-term memory a physical criterion independent of awareness
span.quote: One might relate short-term memory to a pattern of neural firing that represents a particular idea and one might consider the idea to be in short-term memory only when the firing pattern, or cell assembly, is active ( Hebb, 1949 ).

span.label: the independence rule for a union of two events, S+L−SL, used to split a single recall probability into contributions from two stores
span.quote: This model assumes that, for any particular serial position within a list, the likelihood of successful short-term storage (S) and long-term storage (L) are independent, so that the likelihood of recalling the item is S+L−SL.

span.label: a NON-STUDIED control condition, against list words that were each presented exactly four times; what varied was only how many of those presentations were paired
span.quote: Each word used in the list was presented an equal number of times (four, except in a non-studied control condition) but what varied was how many of those presentations were as singletons and how many were as a consistent pairing.

span.label: short-term → working memory — NO BOUNDARY CAN BE DRAWN - the CONCEPTUAL form of the negative relation (Q-286/Q-287)
span.quote: (1960) used the term “working memory” to refer to temporary memory from a functional standpoint, so from their point of view there is no clear distinction between short-term and working memory.

span.label: working memory — three discrepant definitions named together in one sentence: short-term memory applied to cognitive tasks; a multi-component system; the use of attention to manage short-term memory
span.quote: Working memory has been conceived and defined in three different, slightly discrepant ways: as short-term memory applied to cognitive tasks, as a multi-component system that holds and manipulates information in short-term memory, and as the use of attention to manage short-term memory.

span.label: working memory — Cowan's own sense: short-term memory plus the mechanisms that make use of it
span.quote: What is clear from my definition is that working memory includes short-term memory and other processing mechanisms that help to make use of short-term memory.

span.label: working memory — Engle's sense: the attention-related aspects only, which redefines short-term memory in the same move
span.quote: This definition is different from the one used by some other researchers (e.g., Engle, 2002 ), who would like to reserve the term working memory to refer only to the attention-related aspects of short-term memory.

span.label: working memory — Miller, Galanter and Pribram's original functional sense: memory as it is used to plan and carry out behaviour, with no distinction from short-term memory
span.quote: Miller et al. (1960) used the term “working memory” to refer to temporary memory from a functional standpoint, so from their point of view there is no clear distinction between short-term and working memory.

span.label: short-term memory — broader than primary memory, because a temporarily accessible idea need not have been conscious
span.quote: One difference between the term “short-term memory” and the term “primary memory” is that the latter might be considered to be more restricted. It is possible that not every temporarily accessible idea is, or even was, in conscious awareness.

span.label: short-term memory — as a neural sense: an active cell assembly, whether or not the individual is aware of it
span.quote: One might relate short-term memory to a pattern of neural firing that represents a particular idea and one might consider the idea to be in short-term memory only when the firing pattern, or cell assembly, is active ( Hebb, 1949 ).

span.label: rehearsal — covert verbal (articulatory) versus attention-based; only the first is stopped by articulatory suppression
span.quote: In particular, Cowan (1992) suggested that the process of mentally attending to words or searching through the list, an attention-demanding process, could serve to reactivate items to be recalled in a manner similar to covert verbal rehearsal.

span.label: rehearsal — as even-paced covert articulation versus as a grouping operation; participants asked what they did overwhelmingly reported grouping
span.quote: In fact, Cowan et al. (2006a) asked participants in a digit span experiment how they carried out the task and by far the most common answer among adults was that they grouped the items; participants rarely mentioned saying the items to themselves.

span.label: capacity limit — as duration (items decay from storage over time) versus as number (a ceiling on how many items are held); the paper treats these as the two separable ways stores could differ
span.quote: A duration difference means that items in short-term storage decay from this sort of storage as a function of time. A capacity difference means that there is a limit in how many items short-term storage can hold.

span.label: decay — as gradual degradation of trace quality versus as sudden collapse at a trial-varying moment
span.quote: It may be that decay actually reflects not a gradual degradation of the quality of the short-term memory trace, but a sudden collapse at a point that varies from trial to trial.

span.label: attention in working memory — its control versus its scope; Cowan et al. treat these as independent contributors to aptitude
span.quote: The control of attention is relevant, but there is an independent contribution from the number of items that can be held in attention, or its scope.

span.label: forgetting — as inevitable decay versus as interference during the retention interval, the split that founded the unitary-memory tradition
span.quote: McGeoch (1932) illustrated that forgetting over time was not simply a matter of an inevitable decay of memory but rather of interference during the retention interval; one could find situations in which memory improved, rather than diminish, over time.

span.label: builds-on → Cowan's own earlier theoretical framework (Cowan 1988, 1995, 1999, 2001, 2005)
span.quote: Meanwhile, it may be helpful to summarize a theoretical framework ( Cowan, 1988 , 1995 , 1999 , 2001 , 2005 ) based on past research.

span.label: extends → Baddeley and Hitch's multi-component working memory model
span.quote: Cowan (1988) maintained a multi-component view, like Baddeley and Hitch, but without a commitment to precisely their components

span.label: contradicts → Engle (2002) definition reserving 'working memory' for attention-related aspects of short-term memory
span.quote: This definition is different from the one used by some other researchers (e.g., Engle, 2002 ), who would like to reserve the term working memory to refer only to the attention-related aspects of short-term memory.

span.label: critiques → the field's use of the term working memory, which the paper diagnoses as a usage dispute rather than a substantive disagreement
span.quote: This, however, is not so much a debate about substance, but rather a slightly confusing discrepancy in the usage of terms.

span.label: critiques → Miller's magical number seven, on the authority of Miller's own later account of it
span.quote: However, his autobiographical essay ( Miller, 1989 ) indicates that he was never very serious about the number seven; it was a rhetorical device that he used to tie together the otherwise unrelated strands of his research for a talk.

span.label: contradicts → the unitary-memory tradition (Melton, Crowder, Nairne, Lewandowsky and others) which holds that one set of principles covers memory at every timescale
span.quote: This perspective has been maintained and developed over the years by a steady line of researchers believing in the unity of memory, including, among others, Melton (1963) , Bjork and Whitten (1974) , Wickelgren (1974) , Crowder (1982 , 1993) , Glenberg and Swanson (1986) , Brown et al. (2000) , Nairne (2002) , Neath and Surprenant (2003) , and Lewandowsky et al. (2004) .

span.label: extends → Baddeley and Hitch's multi-component working memory, kept as a shape but not as a component list
span.quote: Cowan (1988) maintained a multi-component view, like Baddeley and Hitch, but without a commitment to precisely their components; instead, the basic subdivisions of working memory were said to be the short-term storage components (activated memory along with the focus of attention within it, shown in Fig. 1 ) and central executive processes that manipulate stored information.

span.label: critiques → Cocchini et al.'s conclusion that dissimilar memory loads do not interfere, which would argue against a general cross-domain store
span.quote: Cocchini et al. (2002) suggested that there is little or no interference between dissimilar lists. If so, that would appear to provide an argument against the presence of a general, cross-domain, short-term memory store. Morey and Cowan (2004 , 2005) questioned this conclusion.

span.label: critiques → Vogel et al. (2005), for splitting participants on the same signal used as the dependent measure
span.quote: One limitation of the study is that the separation of participants into high versus low span was based on the CDA also, and the task used to measure the CDA inevitably required selective attention (to one half of the display) on every trial, whether or not it included objects of an irrelevant color.

span.label: supports → Broadbent's and Cowan's revision of the capacity limit from seven to three or four units
span.quote: Later studies suggested that the limit in capacity is more typically only three or four units ( Broadbent, 1975 ; Cowan, 2001 ).

span.label: RETRACTED (THE SPAN DENIES THE EQUIVALENCE IN ITS OWN LAST CLAUSE) · primary memory —renamed-across-fields→ short-term memory
span.quote: Short-term memory is related to the primary memory of James (1890) and is a term that Broadbent (1958) and Atkinson and Shiffrin (1968) used in slightly different ways.

span.label: episodic buffer —same-as→ focus of attention
span.quote: Baddeley’s (2000) episodic buffer is possibly the same as the information saved in Cowan’s focus of attention, or at least is a closely similar concept.

span.label: phonological loop —part-of→ activated memory
span.quote: By Cowan’s account, Baddeley’s (1986) phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad would be viewed as just two of many aspects of activated memory, which are susceptible to interference to a degree that depends upon the similarity between features of the activated and interfering information sources.

span.label: focus of attention —part-of→ activated memory
span.quote: A subset of the activated information is the focus of attention, which appears to be limited in chunk capacity (how many separate items can be included at once).

span.label: short-term memory —part-of→ long-term memory
span.quote: In this framework, short-term memory is derived from a temporarily activated subset of information in long-term memory.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · temporal decay —distinct-from→ chunk capacity limits
span.quote: Chen and Cowan (2005) showed that the time limit and chunk capacity limit in short-term memory are separate.

span.label: temporal distinctiveness —contrasted-with→ temporal decay
span.quote: Last, it has been argued that the loss of memory over time is not necessarily the result of decay. Instead, it can be caused by temporal distinctiveness in retrieval.

span.label: interference —contrasted-with→ temporal decay
span.quote: McGeoch (1932) illustrated that forgetting over time was not simply a matter of an inevitable decay of memory but rather of interference during the retention interval; one could find situations in which memory improved, rather than diminish, over time.

span.label: chunk capacity limits —distinct-from→ memory span
span.quote: Although it is true that memory span is approximately seven items in adults, there is no guarantee that each item is a separate entity.

span.label: covert verbal rehearsal —distinct-from→ attention-based rehearsal
span.quote: The key difference is that it would not be expected that articulatory suppression would prevent that type of rehearsal. Instead, to prevent that type of rehearsal an attention-demanding task would have to be used.

span.label: covert verbal rehearsal —operationalised-as→ articulatory suppression
span.quote: Therefore, steps have been taken to eliminate rehearsal through a process termed articulatory suppression, in which a simple utterance such as the word “ the” is repeatedly pronounced by the participant during part or all of the short-term memory task (e.g., Baddeley et al., 1975 ).

span.label: control of attention —distinct-from→ scope of attention
span.quote: The control of attention is relevant, but there is an independent contribution from the number of items that can be held in attention, or its scope.

span.label: control of attention —operationalised-as→ antisaccade task
span.quote: For example, Kane et al. found that working memory span storage-and-processing tasks correlates well with the ability to inhibit the natural tendency to look toward a suddenly appearing stimulus and instead to look the other way, the antisaccade task.

span.label: working memory —operationalised-as→ contralateral delay activity
span.quote: Vogel et al. (2005) used a visual array task modified for use with a component of event-related potentials that indicates storage in visual working memory, termed contralateral delay activity (CDA).

span.label: central executive —part-of→ working memory
span.quote: Their thinking led to an influential model ( Baddeley, 1986 ) in which verbal-phonological and visual-spatial representations were held separately, and were managed and manipulated with the help of attention-related processes, termed the central executive.

span.label: short-term memory —part-of→ working memory
span.quote: What is clear from my definition is that working memory includes short-term memory and other processing mechanisms that help to make use of short-term memory.

span.label: chunk capacity limits —operationalised-as→ running memory span
span.quote: For example, in running memory span, a long list of items is presented with an unpredictable endpoint, making grouping impossible.

span.label: sensory memory —distinct-from→ categorical memory
span.quote: Sperling (1960) famously illustrated the difference between unlimited sensory memory and capacity-limited categorical memory.

span.label: temporal decay —distinct-from→ chunk capacity limits
span.quote: Long- and short-term memory could differ in two fundamental ways, with only short-term memory demonstrating (1) temporal decay and (2) chunk capacity limits.

span.label: interaction effect
span.quote: Just as predicted, there was a significant interaction between the response cue and the length of the first half of the response intervals.

span.label: mean
span.quote: In contrast, when the timing of recall had to match the timing of the list presentation, performance was better with a short first half ( M = .70) than with a long first half ( M = .67).

span.label: M
span.quote: performance was better with a short first half ( M = .70) than with a long first half ( M = .67)

span.label: significant interaction
span.quote: Just as predicted, there was a significant interaction between the response cue and the length of the first half of the response intervals.

span.label: S+L−SL
span.quote: the likelihood of successful short-term storage (S) and long-term storage (L) are independent, so that the likelihood of recalling the item is S+L−SL

span.label: correlate
span.quote: measures of working memory have been found to correlate with intellectual aptitudes (and especially fluid intelligence) better than measures of short-term memory

span.label: mathematical model
span.quote: A mathematical model was used to estimate the proportion of recalled pairs that could be attributed to the learned association (i.e., to a two-word chunk) as opposed to separate recall of the two words in a pair.

span.label: Reviewing the evidence, the chapter concludes that the chunk capacity limit is well supported whereas temporal decay remains unsettled.
span.quote: The question of decay is still pretty much open to debate, whereas there is growing support for a chunk capacity limit.

span.label: The real capacity limit is about three to four units rather than Miller's seven, once chunking and rehearsal strategies are controlled.
span.quote: Later studies suggested that the limit in capacity is more typically only three or four units

span.label: Time-based and chunk-based limits are dissociable: which one governs recall depends on list length and on whether recall is free or strictly serial.
span.quote: Chen and Cowan (2005) showed that the time limit and chunk capacity limit in short-term memory are separate.

span.label: A procedure that blocks both articulatory and attention-based rehearsal by requiring recall to match presentation timing produced the interaction predicted by decay.
span.quote: This, then, suggests there could be decay in short-term memory.

span.label: With sensory memory masked, the capacity limit is the same three-to-four items whether stimuli come from one modality or two, supporting a central cross-modal store.
span.quote: The limit of the focus of attention was again shown to be between three and four items, for either unimodal visual or bimodal stimuli.

span.label: Dual-task interference is modality-specific during encoding but modality-general during post-cue retention, implying an abstract storage phase.
span.quote: However, the retention of information following the cue showed dual-task effects that were not modality-specific.

span.label: Because the four-item limit appears in vision and audition despite very different sensory persistence, it is a capacity limit and not a transfer-rate limit.
span.quote: Given the striking differences between Sperling and Darwin et al. in the time period available for the transfer of information to a categorical form, the common four-item limit is best viewed as a capacity limit rather than a rate limit.

span.label: Individual capacity varies from roughly two to six items in adults and predicts cognitive aptitude.
span.quote: Individuals differ in capacity, which ranges from about two to six items in adults (and fewer in children), and the individual capacity limit is a strong correlate of cognitive aptitude.

span.label: Whether short-term memory and working memory are distinct is argued to be largely a terminological rather than substantive dispute.
span.quote: In sum, the question of whether short-term memory and working memory are different may be a matter of semantics.

span.label: the capacity limit is more typically three or four units, not seven
span.quote: Later studies suggested that the limit in capacity is more typically only three or four units ( Broadbent, 1975 ; Cowan, 2001 ).

span.label: Miller was never serious about seven — by his own later account it was a rhetorical device to tie unrelated strands of research together for a talk
span.quote: However, his autobiographical essay ( Miller, 1989 ) indicates that he was never very serious about the number seven; it was a rhetorical device that he used to tie together the otherwise unrelated strands of his research for a talk.

span.label: individual capacity ranges from about two to six items in adults and is a strong correlate of cognitive aptitude
span.quote: Individuals differ in capacity, which ranges from about two to six items in adults (and fewer in children), and the individual capacity limit is a strong correlate of cognitive aptitude.

span.label: visual and auditory experiments give the same four-item limit despite a four-fold difference in sensory decay time, which makes it a capacity and not a rate
span.quote: Given the striking differences between Sperling and Darwin et al. in the time period available for the transfer of information to a categorical form, the common four-item limit is best viewed as a capacity limit rather than a rate limit.

span.label: with both modalities masked, the focus of attention held between three and four items whether the stimuli were unimodal visual or bimodal
span.quote: The limit of the focus of attention was again shown to be between three and four items, for either unimodal visual or bimodal stimuli.

span.label: encoding shows modality-specific dual-task costs but post-cue retention does not, so storage after encoding may be abstract
span.quote: After the initial encoding, working memory storage across several seconds thus may occur abstractly, in the focus of attention.

span.label: Lewandowsky et al. found no decay across response intervals from 400 to 1600 ms under articulatory suppression
span.quote: Despite that suppression, they observed no difference in performance with the time between items in the response varying between 400 and 1600 ms (or between conditions in which the word “super” was pronounced one, two, or three times between consecutive items in the response). They found no evidence of memory decay.

span.label: when recall timing had to match presentation timing, a long first half of the response intervals hurt recall (.67 vs .70)
span.quote: In contrast, when the timing of recall had to match the timing of the list presentation, performance was better with a short first half ( M = .70) than with a long first half ( M = .67).

span.label: the Peterson delay effect disappears on the first few trials and when delays are tested in separate blocks, which attributes much of it to proactive interference
span.quote: On the first few trials, the delay does not matter ( Keppel and Underwood, 1962 ) and no detrimental effect of delay is observed if delays of 5, 10, 15, and 20 s are tested in separate trial blocks ( Turvey et al., 1970 ; Greene, 1996 ).

span.label: with one trial per participant, an effect of delay appears within the first 5 s but not beyond
span.quote: They found an effect of the test delay within the first 5 s but not at longer delays.

span.label: Korsakoff amnesics are spared at the last serial positions in immediate recall but impaired at all positions in delayed recall
span.quote: In delayed recall, the amnesic patients show a deficit at all serial positions, as one would expect if short-term memory for the end of the list is lost as a function of a filled delay period ( Glanzer and Cunitz, 1966 ).

span.label: when recalling from a long-term category such as US states, people produce items in spurts of about three
span.quote: When people must recall items from a category in long-term memory, such as the states of the United States, they do so in spurts of about three items on average.

span.label: capacity estimated at about 3.5 chunks in every learning condition, with prior exposure changing the chunk composition rather than the number
span.quote: This model suggested that the capacity limit was about 3.5 chunks in every learning condition, but that the ratio of two-word chunks to one-word chunks increased as a function of the number of prior exposures to the pairs in the list.

span.label: in adults asked how they did a digit span task, grouping was by far the most common answer and saying the items to themselves was rarely mentioned
span.quote: In fact, Cowan et al. (2006a) asked participants in a digit span experiment how they carried out the task and by far the most common answer among adults was that they grouped the items; participants rarely mentioned saying the items to themselves.

span.label: at four items per second in running span, instructions to rehearse make performance worse rather than better
span.quote: In fact, with a fast presentation rate in running span, instructions to rehearse the items is detrimental, not helpful, to performance ( Hockey, 1973 ).

span.label: the time limit and the chunk capacity limit are separable: long free-recall lists are governed by capacity, short strictly-scored serial lists by time
